sampling_model.design: A fixed-budget two-batch rule assigns the first fraction \(\rho\) according to known variance-only weights \(w\), eliminates the lowest first-batch empirical mean, and assigns the rest proportionally among survivors.
sampling_model.units: For each arm, experimental outcomes are independent Gaussian draws with a fixed unknown mean and a known finite positive arm-specific variance.
sampling_model.treatment: There are \(K\ge3\) mutually exclusive treatment arms, and exactly one treatment is assigned to each sampled unit.
sampling_model.overlap: Every arm receives a positive first-batch fraction, and every survivor receives a positive second-batch fraction.
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: There is no nuisance estimation in the selected kernel because the variance vector is known; unknown-variance adaptation remains outside scope.

comparator_promise_table.comparator_claim: Their sufficient-condition theorem gives strict large-deviation dominance of batched elimination over uniform allocation under a common Gaussian variance.
The GNA-EBA allocation maximizes the worst equal-gap Gaussian exponent using known heterogeneous variances.
An upper large-deviation bound for adaptive sampling proportions transfers to an upper bound for empirical rewards.
SHVar has a finite-budget exponential upper bound under known heterogeneous reward variances.
No fixed-budget algorithm uniformly matches the stronger mean-aware static-oracle exponent for \(K\ge3\) in a regular one-parameter natural exponential family.
Three batches attain asymptotically optimal fixed-confidence sample complexity.

body.tldr: For any \(K\ge3\) and any known finite positive Gaussian variance vector, the variance-aware static equal-gap maximin allocation is strictly dominated, at every unique-best mean vector, by a fully specified proportional two-batch rule that eliminates the lowest first-batch arm and reallocates its remaining share among survivors. The closest same-design result is Imbens, Qin, and Wager’s common-variance batched-elimination dominance theorem; the first changed steps are a heteroskedastic weighted contraction and an exact terminal-branch equality for the coupled two-batch error event. These steps yield the exact finite-branch exponent, a one-dimensional weighted projection coefficient \(C>1\), and matching elimination and terminal witnesses showing that \(\rho^\star=(1+\eta)/(C+\eta)\) delivers the exact proportional-family gain \(G=C(1+\eta)/(C+\eta)>1\). A rounded branchwise Chernoff certificate connects the exponent calculation to finite experimental budgets.

project_justification.gap: The closest same-design result, Imbens, Qin, and Wager’s common-variance batched arm-elimination theorem, gives sufficient conditions for strict large-deviation dominance over uniform allocation. It does not supply the heteroskedastic weighted branch contraction, exact terminal-branch equality, or dominance over Kato’s variance-aware equal-gap maximin allocation.
project_justification.niche: The proportional eliminate-one family preserves the batched-elimination design studied by Imbens, Qin, and Wager while making known arm-specific variances enter every elimination and terminal contraction, so the effect of heterogeneity can be isolated without changing the design motif.
project_justification.fill: The project derives the weighted heteroskedastic contraction and exact coupled terminal-branch equality, then reduces the worst best-elimination event to \(K\) one-dimensional piecewise-quadratic calculations, proves a whole-positive-orthant gain, and certifies the exact maximin timing within the proportional family.

body.related_work: Imbens, Qin, and Wager are the closest same-design comparator: under a common Gaussian variance, their batched arm-elimination result gives sufficient conditions for strict large-deviation dominance over uniform allocation. The first changed steps here are the heteroskedastic weighted contraction of the elimination branches and exact equality for the coupled terminal branches; these steps also permit the comparator to change from uniform allocation to Kato’s generalized Neyman allocation. Kato derives that variance-aware comparator from a worst equal-gap Gaussian experiment, without asserting its pointwise admissibility away from equal gaps. Wang, Tzeng, and Proutiere provide an adaptive large-deviation upper-bound technique, while their explicit completeness caveat leaves room for the finite-branch equality proved here. Lalitha et al. show how known heterogeneous variances should alter elimination allocations and provide finite-budget bounds; their stagewise analysis informs the supporting certificate but is not used as an exact exponent comparator. Goldberger rules out universal matching of the stronger mean-aware static oracle, which is consistent with this paper because \(w\) depends only on variances and is deliberately weaker. Jin et al. optimize a fixed-confidence batched criterion, whereas this paper solves an exact fixed-budget robust-gain game in a two-batch subclass.
body.technical_internal_limitation: The finite-budget quantity \(B_T\) is an upper certificate for the adaptive design's error probability. Comparing it with another upper certificate does not by itself prove finite-sample risk dominance. The theorem-level dominance claim is therefore confined to exact large-deviation exponents.
body.honest_scope: The exact finite-branch equality, weighted projection inequality, whole-positive-orthant dominance, and matching proportional-family witnesses are all proof obligations. The early exact-algebra check at \(s=(1,1,4)\) supports rather than proves the general theorem. Optimality in \(\mathfrak D_2^{\mathrm{all}}\), unknown-variance adaptation, non-Gaussian outcomes, variance ratios changing with \(T\), and finite-sample risk dominance remain open. The equal-variance proposition and the failure of strict gain at \(K=2\) are required reductions.
